---
title: "Research"
---

Our work is grounded in the **exposome framework**: the idea that health is shaped by the full set of environmental exposures a person experiences over the life course. We focus on cities, and on urban nature in particular, treating it as a multidimensional exposure (biodiversity, accessibility, quality, and how people experience it) rather than a single greenness score.

::: theme-grid

::: theme-card
### Measuring urban nature at scale
We build and validate tools that ask not just *whether* nature is present, but whether it is the kind of nature that matters for health. This includes the RECITAL urban green space quality assessment tool and a satellite-based deep learning approach to map green space quality across the continental United States.
:::

::: theme-card
### Urban nature and healthy aging
We link novel nature metrics, including bird biodiversity, to cardiometabolic risk, frailty, biological aging, and cognitive health using large-scale electronic health records.
:::

::: theme-card
### The urban exposome and disparities
We evaluate how natural, built, and social environments jointly shape health trajectories, and how unequal exposures contribute to disparities in healthy aging.
:::

::: theme-card
### Air pollution mixtures
We look beyond PM~2.5~ mass to its chemical components and sources, including exposures related to the World Trade Center disaster, and their links to cardiometabolic and cardiovascular outcomes, even below current regulatory thresholds.
:::

::: theme-card
### Collaborative studies
We provide epidemiologic and geospatial support to clinician-led studies, for example on the role of air pollution in liver transplant outcomes.
:::

:::

## Methods we use

Geospatial exposure assessment · electronic health records · environmental mixture methods · satellite imagery and deep learning · spatial and causal epidemiology
